column1: What is the stoichiometric air-fuel ratio for gasoline combustion by mass?
column2: Approximately 14.7:1 (14.7 grams of air per gram of gasoline) — the chemically ideal ratio for complete combustion.

column1: What is the key architectural difference between a carburetor and electronic fuel injection in terms of control strategy?
column2: Carburetors use passive mechanical metering (Bernoulli's principle through a venturi with fixed jets) with no real-time feedback, while EFI uses active closed-loop control via electronically actuated injectors that can sense and correct actual air-fuel ratio in real time.

column1: Rich vs. lean mixture: what AFR/lambda values define each, and what is the practical tradeoff?
column2: Rich = lambda < 1, AFR below 14.7 (maximizes power, excess fuel cools against detonation). Lean = lambda > 1, AFR above 14.7 (improves fuel economy/emissions but raises combustion temperature).

column1: What are the three fundamental sequential operations an ignition system must perform each cycle?
column2: 1) Accumulate electromagnetic energy in the coil primary during dwell. 2) Collapse the magnetic field at the precise crank angle to induce high voltage in the secondary winding (Faraday's law). 3) Deliver the voltage pulse to the spark plug to ionize the mixture and initiate flame kernel propagation.

column1: Why must ignition advance increase dramatically with RPM (e.g., ~10° BTDC at idle vs. 40°+ BTDC at 13,000 RPM)?
column2: Because flame front propagation speed is roughly constant in time, but at higher RPM there is less crankshaft time per combustion event, so the spark must fire earlier (more crank degrees before TDC) to still achieve peak cylinder pressure ~15-20° after TDC.

column1: What is the fundamental conservation law that governs gear ratios in a transmission?
column2: Conservation of energy: a gearbox cannot create power, only trade torque for angular velocity reciprocally (minus mechanical losses as heat) — torque multiplication by ratio R means speed reduction by the same factor R.

column1: How is the total reduction ratio from crankshaft to rear wheel calculated in a motorcycle drivetrain?
column2: It is the product of three cascaded stages: primary drive ratio × gearbox internal ratio × final drive ratio (e.g., 1.84 × 2.46 × 2.47 ≈ 11.17:1 in first gear).

column1: Why does a narrow engine powerband demand tighter gear ratio spacing compared to a broad torque curve?
column2: A narrow powerband requires the rider to stay close to peak torque RPM between shifts, so tighter ratio spacing prevents the engine from dropping below the effective power range after each upshift; a broad torque curve tolerates wider spacing and fewer shifts.

column1: Distinguish sprung mass from unsprung mass in motorcycle suspension, and why does their ratio matter?
column2: Sprung mass = chassis, engine, bodywork, rider (supported by springs). Unsprung mass = wheels, tires, brakes, fork lowers, swingarm, shock linkage (must follow road surface directly). A lower unsprung-to-sprung mass ratio improves tire contact patch consistency and traction fidelity.

column1: What are the three competing mechanical objectives that motorcycle suspension must simultaneously satisfy?
column2: 1) Absorb high-frequency pavement irregularities without transmitting vibration to the chassis. 2) Resist dive/squat during acceleration and braking to maintain chassis attitude and steering geometry. 3) Control compression/rebound rate to prevent oscillation that breaks tire contact patch adhesion.

column1: State Pascal's Law and its direct consequence for hydraulic motorcycle brakes.
column2: Pressure applied to an enclosed fluid transmits equally in all directions/points of the system. Consequence: lever force at a small master cylinder piston generates pressure (P = F/A) that is transmitted unchanged to larger caliper pistons, producing mechanically multiplied clamping force (Output Force = P × A_caliper).

column1: What causes a 'spongy' brake lever feel, and why is it a critical diagnostic red flag?
column2: Any compressible volume in the hydraulic circuit (air bubble, degraded/compliant hose, or water-contaminated fluid with reduced boiling point) consumes lever travel before useful pressure develops, since Pascal's law assumes an incompressible fluid — this must be resolved before high-speed braking.
